data.text: Phase A integrated on main (integrator, 2026-09-07): the Woodcase un-pin is squash-merged and committed with the soak default raised to 600 s. Suite over the merged tree: 3761 tests in 392 suites passed in 50 s; swiftformat clean. Three criteria marked passed; the Penumbra criterion stays pending for phase B, which builds Penumbra against main. The soak finding (WebKit tail widens under --load 6 because page building no longer takes turns with WebKit on one actor) is recorded in project/2026-09-07-unpinning-and-the-loaded-soak.md; "the pin was an accidental throttle" is the best-supported reading, not proven — flagged to Ben.

Phase B (Penumbra against Woodcase b92181b). The plan's premise was wrong in two ways,
and the real work turned out to be two lines.

**Penumbra does not build against Woodcase main, and has not since 2026-08-29.**
`xcodebuild build` fails with 31 errors, every one of them .pen 2.17 model drift —
`PenStroke`, `PenTextContent`, `PenStrokeThickness` deleted, `PenValue<String>` has no
`.plain`, `Kind.iconFont` renamed to `.icon`, `GroupData` lost `layout`/`width`/`height`/
`gap`/`padding`, `PenImageFill.url` optional — across PropertyFormatter, five
Inspector*Section files, NodeIcon, PenNode+DisplayName, ImageURLScanner and
DragController. Penumbra's own `project/2026-08-29-pen-2.17-adoption.md` (untracked, never
filed in job) describes exactly this port and says it carries four product decisions.
Criterion yX7 ("Penumbra builds and its tests pass") therefore cannot be met by any
un-pin work; `xcodebuild test` cancels at the build. Not touched: that port is a
different leaf and its decisions are Ben's.

**The un-pin breaks nothing in Penumbra, because Penumbra is not in Swift 6 language
mode.** It builds with `-default-isolation=MainActor` and
`-enable-upcoming-feature NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault`, and its concurrency
diagnostics are Swift 5 warnings (eight pre-existing ones, all "main actor-isolated X
from a nonisolated context"). Passing a now-non-Sendable EditableDocument into the
`DocumentPipeline` actor produces no diagnostic at all. So my own §9 list — hoist the
pipeline's reads, change RenderPipeline to take a PenDocument, move AbsoluteRectBuilder
and ExpandedIDMapper — was solving a compile error that does not exist.

**What the un-pin does do is open one real race, invisible to that build.** Every read of
the document inside the pipeline actor is already wrapped in `await MainActor.run` —
except the two `materializeSnapshot()` calls (DocumentPipeline.swift:54 and :128). That
method used to hop to the main actor itself; since b92181b it runs on its caller's
isolation, which there is the pipeline actor, so the CoW copy would be taken off the
actor that owns the document while the main actor may be mutating it. Fixed by passing
`isolation: MainActor.shared` at both call sites — two lines, restoring exactly the old
semantics (copy on main, tree walk detached) with no signature or structural change. The
large refactor is not needed and would have been unverifiable anyway with the suite
unbuildable.

`PenumbraDocument`'s two document `nonisolated(unsafe)` holders are gone as intended:
`_parsedDocument` is a plain `nonisolated let` (PenDocument is Sendable, and it is written
once in init), `_editableDocument` is `@MainActor private var`. `_cachedSnapshot` keeps
its `nonisolated(unsafe)` — it is `Data`, written on main and read from a background
thread by `snapshot(contentType:)`, a genuine cross-thread cache unrelated to the
document and not this leaf's to redesign; worth its own look.

Method note: with the build red for unrelated reasons, "no isolation errors" proves
nothing on its own, so both claims were controlled. A deliberate type error in
PenumbraDocument.swift was reported (the file is type-checked, and all of Penumbra
compiles in one SwiftCompile batch), and a `nonisolated func` constructing an
EditableDocument compiled (so Xcode really is building against the un-pinned Woodcase,
not a cached module).

Phase B outcome (agent opus-unpin, 2026-09-07). Penumbra edited in place, four working-tree files, none of Ben's staged files touched, index untouched, not committed: PenumbraDocument.swift drops both nonisolated(unsafe) document holders (_parsedDocument → nonisolated let; _editableDocument → @MainActor var); DocumentPipeline.swift passes `isolation: MainActor.shared` to its two materializeSnapshot calls — the only real exposure, since that method used to hop to main itself and now runs on its caller (the pipeline actor); CanvasArchitecture.md's "brief MainActor hop" sentence rewritten; a gotcha added to Penumbra's project/gotchas.md. Proposed commit message is in the agent's report; Ben commits.

Criterion "Penumbra builds and its tests pass" is NOT met and cannot be by this leaf: Penumbra has not built against Woodcase main since 2026-08-29 — 31 errors of .pen 2.17 model drift (PenStroke/PenTextContent gone, .iconFont → .icon, GroupData layout fields, Kind.script, PenFill.shader…), identical before and after this change; Penumbra's own untracked project/2026-08-29-pen-2.17-adoption.md describes the port and says it was never filed in job. Controlled: a deliberate type error in PenumbraDocument.swift was reported, and a nonisolated func constructing an EditableDocument compiled — so Xcode is building the un-pinned library and the un-pin itself adds no error. Marked skipped with this waiver; the 2.17 port is Penumbra's leaf, Ben's decisions.

Unexplained and flagged as an issue: under SWIFT_VERSION 6 / strict concurrency complete / approachable concurrency, passing the non-Sendable EditableDocument from the main actor into a DocumentPipeline actor method draws NO diagnostic (verified at the real call site and with a probe). Likeliest reading is SE-0414 region transfer; either way the docs' "the compiler refuses to let it cross" is stronger than what was observed, and Penumbra's MainActor.run discipline in the pipeline is load-bearing.

data.title: Sending a non-Sendable EditableDocument into an actor method draws no diagnostic
data.description:
Found during the un-pin (leaf 111nTf, phase B in Penumbra, 2026-09-07). Penumbra's DocumentPipeline is an `actor` whose methods take `editableDocument: EditableDocument` — a non-Sendable class since b92181b — and calling them from the main actor draws no diagnostic under SWIFT_VERSION 6, SWIFT_STRICT_CONCURRENCY complete, SWIFT_APPROACHABLE_CONCURRENCY YES. Verified at the real call site and with a deliberate probe. The likeliest reading is SE-0414 region-based isolation transferring the value's region at the call, but that is not established.

Why it matters: EditingDocuments.md ("Who owns a document"), EditableDocument's Isolation section and EditingIsolationTests all say the compiler refuses to let a document cross an isolation boundary. If a send into an actor method is accepted, that guarantee is narrower than the docs state — the sender may just lose the right to use the value afterwards, or nothing may be checked at all — and Penumbra's `MainActor.run` discipline inside the pipeline is load-bearing rather than redundant.

To do: reproduce in a Woodcase test (an actor taking EditableDocument, called from another isolation; does it compile? does a use-after-send error fire?), state precisely what the compiler does and does not guard, and correct the three places above so they claim exactly that. Answer belongs in a dated project doc.

data.text:
Design decisions settled while building the read-only host (opus-host-core, 2026-09-07).

(a) The `doc` Proxy. `doc` is a Proxy over an internal `api` object; the member table
`MEMBERS` in the prelude is the single source of truth for the Proxy's sentences, the
option checks and `ScriptHost.members()`. Unknown member: "doc has no setProps — its
members are rev, tree, get, lint, schema; `woodcase help js` prints them". Unknown option:
"doc.tree has no option position — the options it takes are depth, expand, props, theme;
`woodcase help js` prints them"; a member with no options gets "doc.schema takes no
options, and was given verbose." A `retired` table gives a *better* sentence for CLI flags
that are only about printing: `tree.absolute` ("every row already carries both rect and
absRect"), `lint.summary`, `lint.list`, `get.instances`. Symbol reads and a short
PASSTHROUGH list (toJSON, then, toString, valueOf, constructor, inspect) return undefined
rather than throwing, so `console.log(doc)` and `await doc` do not explode. Assignment to
`doc` is refused. Option *shape* is checked in the prelude and the Swift side trusts it;
Swift checks only *vocabulary* it alone knows — lint check ids and node type names.

(b) console. log/warn/error, plus info and debug as aliases of log (a model reaches for
them and a bare TypeError teaches nothing; the level vocabulary stays three). Arguments
join with spaces; strings verbatim; objects/arrays via JSON.stringify; undefined/null
spelled out; a function renders "[function name]"; an Error renders "Name: message"; a
cycle renders "[unprintable: …]" rather than throwing inside a log call.

(c) No event loop. setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, queueMicrotask, clearTimeout,
clearInterval, fetch, XMLHttpRequest and require all throw `code: 'synchronousOnly'` and
share one clause — "a woodcase script runs to completion in one pass, with no event loop,
because the whole run is one file transaction and the file lock cannot outlive it" —
followed by the remedy that fits (do the work inline / pass it in from the shell / put
shared code in a file and `-F helpers.js -F run.js`). `import`/`export` cannot be
intercepted by a global: they are statements, so the parse fails first. A SyntaxError
whose source has a top-level import/export is re-described with the modules sentence and
the same code. A Promise as the completion value yields a null result plus a warning
naming the same clause.

(d) WoodcaseError. A JS class defined in the prelude with `message`, `code` and
`candidates`. Every Swift-side throw is constructed *through* the prelude's own
`makeError`, so `catch (e) { e instanceof WoodcaseError }` holds for a refusal raised in
Swift exactly as for one raised in JS. `code` is `EditingError.code` (new public
`var code: String` on the library error, spelled out rather than reflected) for anything
the editing layer threw, and otherwise one of `ScriptErrorCode`'s: timeout, syntaxError,
unknownMember, unknownOption, badArgument, synchronousOnly, unknownNodeType,
sourceUnreadable, scriptError. `candidates` comes from a new public
`EditingError.candidates` covering ambiguousAddress, addressNotFound and
overrideTargetNotFound. The sentence itself is `BatchErrorMessage.describe` — no second
prose anywhere — and which grammar the remedy uses is a new `remedy: RemedyDialect`
parameter on `ScriptHost.run`, which the `js` verb will pass as `.command(file: path)`.

(e) ScriptRun.Commit is defined now with all four cases (wrote, unchanged, previewed,
rolledBack). The read-only host reports `unchanged` on a clean run and `rolledBack` when a
run ends in an error — the distinction a reader needs is *why* nothing was written, and it
stays true when the write side lands, since the whole run is one transaction.

Two contract refinements against the plan's `.d.ts` sketch, both deliberate:
- `theme` is an object (`{ mode: 'dark' }`), not an array of `"axis=value"` strings. The
  library takes `[String: String]`; the string form exists only because argv has no
  objects, and the 2026-09-07 review ruled that argv coercion does not apply to scripts.
  Duplicate axes become impossible and empty values are refused by name.
- `props` takes an array of paths only. The CLI's bare `--props` picks four defaults
  because a *flag* can be written bare; an option key cannot, and `props: true` is refused
  with a sentence that shows the array form. This also keeps `Tree.defaultPropertyPaths`
  in the command core where it belongs.
- `lint` and `tree` both take `(address?, options?)`, matching the verbs' positional
  subtree. An options object in the address slot is redirected: "write
  doc.tree(null, { … }) to read the whole file."

data.label: The target builds under Swift 6 strict concurrency with no warnings, JavaScriptCore never appears in the Woodcase target, and no global-actor annotation appears in the host
A run over a file source and a text source in order shares one context, and an error in either is reported with that source's name
A run from a non-main actor works, and the sink receives events in the order the timeline records them
A script whose completion value is a function, a Promise or a cycle yields a null result and a warning event, never an unreadable string
setTimeout, fetch and require each throw the synchronous-scripts sentence, and an error in the second of two sources reports that source's name and line
doc.tree, doc.get, doc.lint and doc.schema return the same values the corresponding verbs print with --json, proven by a parity test over the batch.pen fixture
An ambiguous or missing address thrown into the script carries code, the verb's own sentence and a candidates array the script can read
Accessing an unknown member of doc throws a sentence naming every real member, and an unknown option key names the keys that member takes
A script past its deadline receives a catchable timeout error on its next doc call, asserted on outcome and not on elapsed time
An uncaught error is reported with its line, column and quoted source line

data.text:
Decisions taken while building out-of-band detection + undo-by-transaction (opus-external).

**The lineage comparison is one library type.** `Sources/Woodcase/Files/LogLineage.swift`:
an enum with three answers — `unlogged` (no history: never a divergence), `current(event)`,
`diverged(since:found:)` — plus `explains(_:at:)`, which is the bare `event.revision ==
documentRevision` that `UndoStep.decide` used to inline. The transaction asks it once per
open; undo asks `explains` of every candidate. The type also owns the two things derived
from a divergence: `note(naming:)` (the sentence) and `external(naming:at:)` (the row).

**stepOverUndone stays.** The brief allowed removing it if the external row made it
unnecessary; it does not. The heuristic exists so a *second* undo can walk past an event
an earlier undo already reversed — a revision mismatch the log genuinely explains — and no
external row is involved in that case. What the row removes is the heuristic's documented
*cost*: an outside edit used to hide behind it as "nothing left to undo"; now it has a row
and its own refusal. `UndoStep`'s doc comment says exactly this under "The one heuristic,
and why it stayed".

**Undo's shape in the library.** `ActivityUndo.reverse(in:through:editing:log:identity:
allIdentities:limit:unit:) -> ActivityUndo.Result` (undone, stopped, recorded) plus public
`UndoStep` and `UndoUnit` — all in Sources/Woodcase/Files/. `UndoCommand` keeps argv,
`UndoReport` and `UndoFailures` (formatting; `blocked(_:)` gained a `.blockedByExternal`
sentence). Events already recorded by the transaction — i.e. the pending external row —
count as the newest part of the tail, which is what lets an undo refuse to step past an
outside edit it is the first to notice.

**Undo by transaction is a walk, not a grouping.** First cut grouped events by batch id and
judged each group by its last event. That broke composition: after `undo --event` took the
last row of a six-row `cp --times 3`, a plain `undo` judged the group by that already
reversed row and answered "nothing to undo" with five rows plainly left. The shipped walk
is one event at a time — each row judged on its own revision, so each inverse stays exact —
and the batch id decides only whether the next row *counts* against `-n`. Same result for
an intact transaction, right result for a half-undone one.

**Two findings from the suite.**

`woodcase find` is built, on branch `agent-a6e35117a3f8b5d41` (worktree of the same name). Suite: 3902 tests / 409 suites pass (`swift test --quiet`), `swiftformat . --config .swiftformat --lint` clean.

**Shape.** `find <file> [<node>] [<predicate>] [-F <file>] [--props …] [--expand] [--absolute] [--json]`. The verb opens the file with `PenFileTransaction.read`, builds `TreeView.rows` exactly as `tree` does, warns about empty `--props` columns exactly as `tree` does, filters through `RowPredicate`, and prints through `TreeFormatter` — so `find 'r => true'` is byte-for-byte `tree`, in text and in `--json`, and a filtered set is `TreeFormatter`'s own bytes for those rows. Exit 0 matches / 1 none (nothing on stdout, in either form) / 2 predicate or address / 4 file.

**New library type:** `WoodcaseScripting.RowPredicate` (+ `RowPredicatePrelude`), a fresh `JSContext` with no `doc`, the predicate compiled once, rows crossing as one `ScriptJSON` array. `WoodcaseCommandCore` gained the `WoodcaseScripting` dependency in Package.swift.

**Three decisions worth the record.**

1. *The transcript in the plan doc was not a form `tree` prints* — its second column was each row's path, and it carried no header. The contract one paragraph below it says `tree`'s own format and `--json` shape, so the format won and the transcript is corrected in place (marked block quote) with a real run against `banking.pen`. `find` prints `tree`'s header too: it carries the revision, which is the thing a query runs to feed to the write that follows.

2. *`r.props` is a view, not a second key.* A `TreeRow` encodes its columns under `properties`; the plan and the brief both write `r.props['kind.fontSize']`. Both spellings now reach one guarded view, so the shorthand exists without a twin key and without leaving `r.properties['not.asked.for']` as a silent `undefined` hole.

3. *The Proxy earns its keep.* `r.fontSize` is `undefined` and `undefined < 12` is `false`, so a plain row would answer "no matches" to a question nobody asked — silently, exit 1. Every row is a Proxy refusing a member the row type does not have, listing the ones it does, and naming the row it happened on; `doc` is a global getter throwing the sentence that points at `js`.

**Deliberately not built** (say so if wanted): `--theme` and `--depth`. Neither is in the brief's grammar; `r.depth` covers the second, but a themed document can only be searched at its default theme until `--theme` lands. Four lines, if it is wanted.

**One thing the grammar cannot do.** With `-F`, a lone operand is always the subtree — ArgumentParser fills the first positional, so `find f.pen 'r=>…' -F p.js` is indistinguishable from `find f.pen Board -F p.js`. The rule is deterministic and documented rather than guessed at by sniffing for an arrow; two operands plus `-F` is refused as two predicates.

data.text:
Decisions taken while building the write side (opus-host-write, 2026-09-07).

**ScriptRun.commit for a run with writes and no error: `.wrote`.**
The host holds an EditableDocument, never a file — it does not encode, compare bytes or
rename — so it answers for *the script*: `.wrote` when at least one `.write` event is on
the timeline, `.unchanged` when none is, `.rolledBack` when the run ended in an uncaught
error (whether or not writes landed on the document first; the run is one transaction, so
an error means the file and the log are untouched). The `js` verb owns the two answers the
host cannot give and maps `PenFileTransaction.Outcome.commit` over this one where they
differ: `.previewed` for `--dry-run`, and `.unchanged` for a script that wrote and wrote
back — the document encodes to the bytes it was handed, so nothing was written after all,
which only the transaction can see. Documented on `ScriptRun.Commit`.

**`vars.rm` / `themes.rm` do not go through `BatchApplier.applyOne`, because they cannot.**
The batch grammar deliberately carries no removal for a variable or a theme axis (an
optional payload on `var` would turn a dropped field into a silent delete), so there is no
`BatchOperation` to translate into. They go where `woodcase vars rm` goes — straight to
`EditOperation.removeVariable` / `.removeThemeAxis` through the recorder, or straight to
`EditableDocument.apply` when there is no recorder. The brief's "each translates its
arguments into the matching BatchOperation" is true of the other nine members only.

**`doc.vars.rm` mirrors the verb's refusal, and the sentence is written twice.**
Removing a referenced variable is applied happily by the library — the node renders the
unresolved reference — so the refusal is a *policy*, and it lives in `VarsRemoveCommand`.
The host makes the same decision over the same public fact (`EditableDocument.references(to:)`)
with the remedy in the script's grammar (`{ force: true }`, since a script has no
`--force`). New code `variableInUse`. That leaves the *decision* stated in two modules; the
right fix is a small library type both call, which needs an edit to `VarsRemoveCommand`
(owned by leaf Dy6k8Z this sitting) — filed as an integration note rather than done here.

**`BatchError.documentRevisionConflict` keeps its own code, not `revisionConflict`.**
`BatchError.code` follows `EditingError.code`'s rule — the case's own name. A stale `rev`
on `doc.set`/`mv`/`rm`/`replace`/`override` throws `revisionConflict` as the brief says
(those pin a node); a stale `rev` on a root-level `doc.add`/`doc.cp` pins the whole
document and throws `documentRevisionConflict`. A caller that has to re-read before
retrying needs to know which.

**Contract refinements against the plan's `.d.ts` sketch.**
- `override(address, props, options?)` — one address, not `(instance, descendant, …)`.
  The verb takes one address that walks *through* the instance, and the report names the
  instance.
- `cp` has no `name` option: the CLI has none either; a copy's name is
  `props: { 'common.name': … }`. `times` is CLI sugar over `each`; both are `retired`
  entries with the sentence that redirects.
- No `tag` on `add`/`cp` — a `retired` entry says why the return value replaces it.
- Every write member returns a `WriteReport`, including `vars.*` and `themes.*` (the
  sketch had them `void`); its keys are `nodeRevision`/`documentRevision`, the real type's,
  not the sketch's `rev`.

data.text:
Carve decisions before dispatch (integrator, 2026-09-07 evening).

- **Root-overlap warnings are folded in on the verb side.** The verb takes `RootOverlapWarnings.pairs(in:)` before the run and `lines(since:in:file:)` after it, exactly as apply does, prints them on stderr after the transcript, and carries them under `--json` as `warnings`. The host-side event (a library caller seeing them) is issue ctvJct, not this leaf.
- **The plan's transcript does not run as written and the criterion means the corrected one.** `banking.pen` has `banking-home/transactions-section`, not `banking-home/recent`; a TreeRow member is `address`, not `path`; `cp` has no `name` option (retired — a copy's name is `props: { 'common.name': … }`). Correct the transcript in the plan doc in place as a marked block quote, the way the find leaf corrected its own, and make the criterion's fixture test the corrected script.
- **Exit codes.** Uncaught script error 1 (the check ran and the answer is no; nothing written); a source that will not parse 2 with file, line and message; stale guard, lock timeout and the watchdog 3; unreadable .pen 4; a `-F` path that cannot be read 2 (usage, as apply's is).
- **Commit mapping.** The host answers `.wrote`/`.unchanged`/`.rolledBack` for the script; the verb maps `PenFileTransaction.Outcome.commit` over it: `.previewed` under `--dry-run`, `.unchanged` when the transaction found the bytes identical.
- **The watchdog is a thread, not a Task**, so a `while (true) {}` that never yields cannot starve it; it prints the sentence and calls `exit(3)`. Its grace is a named constant with a doc comment saying why.
- **Contention.** The imports agent (leaf TyiIb1) also adds one line to WoodcaseCommand.swift's subcommand list and one row plus one section to WoodcaseCLI.md; the integrator resolves those two spots.

Carve decisions before dispatch (integrator, 2026-09-07 evening).

- **The "is it referenced" decision moves into the library, once, and this leaf owns it.** `VarsRemoveCommand.refusal(...)` and `ScriptWrite.refuseIfInUse` decide the same fact in two modules (the write agent's note on yp3EcU). Removing an import alias a ref still uses is the same shape a third time. So: one library type in Sources/Woodcase/Editing/ that, given a name and a document, answers the references and renders the refusal sentence in the remedy dialect (`--force` for the command, `{ force: true }` for a script); `vars rm`, `doc.vars.rm`, `imports rm` and `doc.imports.rm` all call it. The command and the script keep only their own remedy words.
- **Batch grammar.** `{"op":"import","alias":ALIAS,"path":PATH}` adds or changes; removal, like `var`, is deliberately not a batch line (a dropped field must not become a delete) — `imports rm` and `doc.imports.rm` go straight to `EditOperation.removeImport` through the recorder, as `vars rm` does.
- **Contention.** The js-verb agent (leaf DESilx) adds one line to WoodcaseCommand.swift's subcommand list and one row plus one section to WoodcaseCLI.md; the integrator resolves those two spots. Do not touch Verbs/JsCommand.swift or anything named Script*Formatter.

Imports on every route, and the one library answer to "is this name still referenced" (opus-imports, 2026-09-07).

**The shared type is `Woodcase.NameInUse` (Sources/Woodcase/Editing/NameInUse.swift).** A `Friendly` struct — `name`, `nodePaths`, `variableNames`, plus `isEmpty`/`count` and `sentence(in: RemedyDialect)` — with two factories that do the walking: `NameInUse.variable(_:in:)` over the existing `EditableDocument.references(to:)`, and `NameInUse.importAlias(_:in:)`, which is new. It holds *name paths*, not node ids, because every caller was already mapping ids through `namePath(of:)` before rendering and nothing else wanted the ids. Four call sites now share it: `VarsRemove`, `ImportsRemove`, `ScriptWrite.remove`'s `.variable` and `.importAlias` branches. `VarsRemoveCommand.refusal/list/listLimit` and `ScriptWrite.refuseIfInUse/list/listLimit` are gone; the two sentences come out byte-identical (pinned in `NameInUseTests`, `VarsCommandTests`, `ScriptWriteTests`).

**`RemedyDialect` gained a third case, `.script`.** The brief said to spell `--force` for `.command` and `{ force: true }` for "the script" and to look at how RemedyDialect already spells the two — it does not: it had only `.batch` and `.command`, and the script route passes `.batch` by default (`ScriptHost.run(remedy:)`) or `.command(file:)` under the `js` verb. Mapping `.batch` onto a JavaScript remedy would have been a lie, and reading `runner.remedy` would print `--force` to a script running under `js`. So `.script` is its own case; `BatchErrorMessage.sentence(_:batch:command:in:)` gives it the batch remedy (`case .batch, .script:`), which is exactly today's behaviour for every other message, and `NameInUse.sentence` is the one place it differs. Nothing changed for any existing caller.

**The alias walk is namespace-shaped, not ref-shaped.** An import aliased `V` prefixes *everything* the library defines (`V:Bt0aA`, `$V:--primary`, the axis `V:Mode`, descendant override keys). Counting only `ref` nodes would have let `imports rm` remove an alias a fill still binds to. So the walk takes a node if it is a `ref` whose target starts `V:`, **or** if any `$`-leaf of its encoded JSON starts `V:` — reusing `EditableDocument.collectReferences(in:into:)`, which went from `private` to `internal` for the purpose rather than being copied. Variables whose own value names the namespace land in `variableNames`, symmetric with the variable case. Prefix collisions are handled by matching `"\(alias):"`, so removing `V` is not refused by a `VV:` reference (test: `aliasesDoNotBleedIntoEachOther`).

**Wrong in the brief, for the record.** (1) `RemedyDialect` as above. (2) "The `.d.ts` in the write agent's report on yp3EcU, section 9" — `job show yp3EcU` carries no `.d.ts` and no numbered sections; the only sketch is in `project/2026-09-07-scripting-host.md` around line 131, and it is out of date there (it has `imports.set/rm` returning `void`; the shipped contract is a `WriteReport`, as the write agent's note itself corrects for `vars.*`). `HNG9g4` should take the runtime (`ScriptHost.members()`) as the source, not that sketch. (3) The brief named three verb files; `vars` uses four (container + list + set + rm) and one-type-per-file means `imports` does too — `ImportsListCommand.swift` is the extra one.

**Fixture.** `Tests/WoodcaseTests/Fixtures/imports.pen` — two aliases, `V` reached by a `ref` and by a `$V:--primary` fill, `icons` reached by nothing. It is the fixture the CLI, batch, script and library suites all share, so the refusal sentence is asserted against one document on every route.

data.text:
Built on wt/js-verb (worktree .claude/worktrees/js-verb). Suite 4015 tests green, swiftformat clean.

**The row has no verb column, and cannot have one.** `ScriptRun.Event.write` carries a
`WriteReport` and nothing that says which member made it, so a transcript row is `path
id (+N)` — a `cp`, a `set` and an `rm` on the same node read identically. This bit the
plan's own transcript: my first corrected script did `cp` then two `override`s per row
and printed three identical lines, because `override` reports the *instance*. The
one-line host change is `case write(verb: String, WriteReport)` (or a `verb` field on
the case) with `operation.verb.rawValue` filled in at ScriptWrite.swift:51 and :90 —
both of which are the imports leaf's file, which is why I did not make it. Issue-worthy;
the primer and the plan doc's transcript both read better with it.

**Fixed one host bug (ScriptFailure.swift, 3 lines + a regression test).** A refusal the
*prelude* raised — `doc.setProps(…)` — took its `source` from the fallback (the user's
file) and its `line`/`column` from the exception (the prelude's line 19), so a one-line
script was reported as `typo.js:19:28`, pointing at a line that does not exist. Line and
column are now taken only when the exception's `sourceURL` maps to a source we
evaluated. `ScriptSynchronyTests.apreludeRefusalIsNotLocatedInTheScript` is the
regression.

**Two brief facts that were wrong, resolved toward the existing code.**
`PenFileTransaction.run(at:identity:…)` takes no `diagnostics:` collector — only
`read(at:diagnostics:)` does — so `doc.lint()` inside `js` reports the linter's own
checks and not the parse's diagnostics, as `apply --dry-run` also does. And an
unreadable `-F` path exits **4**, not 2: `InputFile`'s documented contract is "a body
that cannot be read is targetFailure (4) — the invocation was fine, the world was not",
and that is what `apply -F missing` does today. Consistency with `apply` was the note's
stated reason for its number, so I followed the reason.

**Corrected transcript.** `banking.pen`'s list is `transactions-section`, its rows are
`ref` instances of `component/TransactionItem`, `doc.get` answers a `NodeReport` (so the
parent is `section.node.id`), and a copy's name is `props: {'common.name': …}` — with a
key written as a *path into the copy* (`info/merchant/kind.content`) becoming an
override, which is how one `cp` fills a whole row. The un-filtered `tree` read also
includes the section itself, taller than any row, so the overflow check needed
`r.depth === 1` or it threw every time. The block quote in the plan doc says all of
this; `JsCommandTests.planTranscriptRuns` is the script as a test, and it also asserts
the overrides landed on `vpvCO`, because "the rows printed" alone would not have caught
a `cp` whose props silently no-op'd.

**Decisions.** Report and formatter are two files (`Reports/ScriptRunReport.swift`,
`Reports/ScriptRunFormatter.swift`) rather than one, for the one-type-per-file rule.
JSON carries `events` — one timeline, as the plan argued — with an explicit
discriminated event shape, because `ScriptRun.Event`'s synthesized `Codable` writes
`{"write":{"_0":…}}` and `_0` is not a key a caller should have to know. A dry run and a
rolled-back run print no `document` row and carry no `documentRevision`, exactly as
`WriteReport` and `BatchReport` do — neither made a revision. The dry-run marker is
printed *inside* the transaction after the guards pass, so a refused guard prints no
marker (`DryRunTests` asserts the same for `set`). The watchdog lives in
`Hosting/ScriptWatchdog.swift` beside `ParentProcessWatch`, which is the same kind of
thing; its grace is 2 s with a doc comment saying why, and the cancel/fire race is
closed by holding one `Mutex` across the decision and the `exit`.

Second occurrence, 2026-09-07 20:08–20:20: the full suite over the imports merge on main sat at 0.2 % CPU for 10 min while one Opus agent ran `swift test` in a worktree and another ran `xcodebuild` in the Penumbra sibling worktree. Sample: local/wedge-2026-09-07-imports-merge.sample.txt. Frames of ours: `ChangeCoordinator.start(watcher:)` → `ActivityReader.Follow.Iterator.next()` → `ActivityReader.read` (the poll loop, i.e. what is still moving, not the culprit — gotchas 2026-08-31). Killed by pid; the harness then reported the backgrounded `swift test` as exit 0 with no summary line, which is not a pass. Both occurrences were under three-way build load. Next step if it recurs a third time: raise it with `scripts/soak-tests 2 <log> --load 6` on a quiet machine and look at what the wedged test was awaiting, not at the follow loop.

data.text:
Built on wt/help-js (worktree .claude/worktrees/help-js). Suite 4065 tests in 422 suites green, swiftformat clean, DocC warnings unchanged from main.

**The verb column, as built.** `ScriptRun.Event.write(member:_:)` carries a new public
`ScriptWriteMember` enum rather than the brief's `String`. The formatter has to pad the
column to the widest name any run could print, and `CaseIterable` is what makes that
width a fact about the vocabulary instead of a number chosen in the formatter —
`ScriptWriteMember.columnWidth` (11, `imports.set`). The raw values are the names a
caller writes, so `--json` is exactly the string the brief asked for. `ScriptWrite`'s old
`member(for:)` became `ScriptWriteMember(verb)` plus `qualifiedName` for the one caller
that wants the `doc.` prefix. Divergence rows now indent past the member gutter (13) so a
sentence sits under the path it is about; the quoted source line of a *refusal* keeps its
two-space indent, since stderr has no member column.

**The `.d.ts` is written by hand, held to the runtime by a test.** The prelude's table
knows a member's name, kind and option keys and nothing else — no parameters, no return
types, no meaning — so generating the declaration would have shipped a worse document and
still needed the same test. `JsDeclarationTests` parses the `declare const doc` block and
checks it against `ScriptHost.members()` in both directions, plus the eight retired keys.
It lives in `Tests/WoodcaseCommandTests/Help/` and not beside the prelude because the text
is WoodcaseCommandCore's and the runtime is WoodcaseScripting's: that is the only test
target importing both.

**Both new suites were mutation-checked, not just watched go green.** Adding a
`cascade?: boolean` to `RmOptions` failed `theOptionKeysMatch`; changing the fan-out's `cp`
source to a name the fixture has no node for failed `everyScriptExitsZero` with exit 1.

**A finding the docs leaf should carry: `r.props` does not exist under `js`.** A `find`
predicate sees each row through a Proxy where `r.props` is the guarded shorthand; a row
from `doc.tree()` is a plain `JSON.parse` object whose only bag is `properties`, so
`r.props['kind.fontSize']` reads `undefined` and `undefined < 12` is `false` — the exact
silent-wrong-answer trap `RowPredicatePrelude` exists to prevent, live on the write side.
The topic says so in its SEE ALSO and declares `properties` only. Worth an issue: give
`doc.tree()` rows the same Proxy, or nothing will ever catch it.

**The design primer stayed at 140 lines** by reflowing five paragraphs to ~95 columns
(the width budget is 100 and it was sitting at 89) rather than by dropping teaching.
Two of those reflows broke phrases `DesignTopicClaimsTests` and
`DesignTopicComponentClaimsTests` pin across a line break — "unique among its siblings"
and "`get Inst/Note0` reads one" — which is what those suites are for.

Also added `find` to `HelpCommandTests`' `classedVerbs` and `verbsWithExamples`: the verb
shipped without being in either list, so nothing checked that its abstract states its
class or that its help carries a worked example. Both pass.

data.title: doc.tree() rows are plain objects, so r.props is undefined where find's Proxy would refuse
data.description: A row from `doc.tree()` in a `js` script is a plain JSON.parse object, while a row a `find` predicate sees is the refusing Proxy from RowPredicatePrelude. So `r.props['kind.fontSize']` — the spelling `find` teaches — is `undefined` under `doc.tree()`, and `undefined < 12` is `false`: the silent-wrong-answer trap the Proxy exists to prevent, live on the write side, where a filter that matches nothing means a script that writes nothing and exits 0. `help js` declares `properties` only and says so in SEE ALSO, which is a fence, not a fix. Fix: wrap the rows `doc.tree()` returns in the same Proxy `find` uses (one prelude, both routes), so an unknown member throws the sentence naming the row's members and `r.props` works in both places. Found by the help-js agent (leaf HNG9g4), 2026-09-07.

data.text: Experiment, 2026-09-07 21:00–21:20, main at f174fb4, quiet machine otherwise. Question: do two simultaneous `swift test` runs (main checkout + a worktree) reproduce the wedge? Three rounds, verbose logs in local/wedge-experiment/round{1,2,3}-{a-main,b-worktree}.log. Round 1 was suite A against B's cold build (A 72.6 s, B 50.4 s alone afterwards); rounds 2 and 3 overlapped both test phases fully (70.8/69.9 s, 69.2/67.3 s). No wedge in any of the six runs, and no stall over 30 s. One failure: round 3 suite A, ViewerBrowserTests "Selecting a node scrolls the outline to its row" (the scrollIntoView-sensitive test from gotchas 2026-08-30) — a load flake, 1 of 6. Conclusion: two overlapping suites alone do not wedge; both real wedges had a third load source (an agent's build plus an xcodebuild). Consistent with the August finding that the face is contention-shaped, not a specific shared resource. Next if it recurs: the integrator's suite runs are now verbose to a log (see handoff), so the in-flight tests will be named; then soak-tests --load 6 on that test.

Dispatch decisions, 2026-09-08 (integrator, before the docs agent runs):
- Cross-module symbol links: the catalog is Woodcase's, and the host is WoodcaseScripting, so a ``ScriptHost``-style link may not resolve in a `--target Woodcase` build. The agent measures the catalog's warning baseline first and holds the new article to adding none; the "Scripting symbol group" ships only if DocC resolves it, otherwise the article names the host's types in code voice and says which target they live in (WoodcaseViewer.md is the precedent for a sibling module's article).
- The `.d.ts` in the article is held to `HelpTopic+Js.swift` by a test, and the article's scripts run through the binary the way `JsTopicTests` runs the topic's. A parallel agent (host-fixes) is changing the `.d.ts` (TreeRow gains `props`); the integrator refreshes the article's block at merge time — the test is what makes that safe.
- CLAUDE.md is a symlink to AGENTS.md; the documentation list lives in the project-owned head above the generated regions, so editing it is allowed.

Dispatch decision, 2026-09-08: fixed together with ctvJct by one agent (same target, disjoint files from the docs agent). Shape: one row view shared by find's prelude and doc.tree — a Proxy over the row whose refusal sentence fits the route it is on (find says `--props kind.x`, js says `props: ['kind.x']`). The `.d.ts` in help js declares `props?: Props` on TreeRow beside `properties`, and the SEE ALSO fence sentence goes. The result of a script whose last expression is `doc.tree(...)` must still stringify.

Dispatch decision, 2026-09-08: the pair diff moves into the library beside RootOverlap; ScriptRunner records one `.warning` event per newly overlapping pair once at run end (apply's net-out semantics, not per write), rendered as the verbs print it so `warnings` in `--json` and the stderr lines are byte-identical to today; JsCommand stops diffing on its own and reads the run's events, so no line prints twice.

Dispatch decision, 2026-09-08: PNG output goes to a per-process temporary directory through one shared test helper; no stable human-facing copy (Ben does not treat /tmp as a workspace, and nobody reads these routinely). performance/mae-test.csv, which scripts/mae-check reads, is unaffected and must stay where it is. The font-cache half is a premise check: CoreText registration is process-scoped, so a second *process* cannot flip this process's absent-to-present transition; the agent verifies whether any test reads the real ~/Library/Caches/woodcase and reports rather than building unless one does.

data.title: Greenfield trial: a mobile-first Nanoshoot design
data.description: A second trial, greenfield: an agent designs a mobile-first front end for Nanoshoot (../nanoshoot/, a photographer- and user-facing product that never got a real design) from an empty .pen file, with `woodcase help design` and `woodcase help js` as its only teaching and every route available. Where the Quill trial (ShQWa9) asks whether an agent stays inside the tool on a loop-shaped edit of an existing file, this asks whether the host holds up when there is nothing to copy from: which route it reaches for to build a component library and a set of screens, where it leaves the tool, and which sentences were not enough. Findings land as a dated project doc and each sentence that was not enough becomes an issue. Offered by Ben 2026-09-08; the design itself is a deliverable for Nanoshoot, so the .pen file goes to that repo, not this one.

data.text:
Docs for the scripting host, 2026-09-08 (docs-scribe, worktree wt/docs-scripting).

WHAT SHIPPED
- `Sources/Woodcase/Documentation.docc/WoodcaseScripting.md` — "The JavaScript Host".
  Premise from the plan doc, the three rules, no session, synchronous-and-alone, what
  comes back, refusals, the `declare const doc` block verbatim from `HelpTopic+Js.swift`,
  the Swift API (`ScriptHost.run`, `ScriptRun`/`Event`, `ScriptSource`, `ScriptError`/
  `ScriptErrorCode`, the sink, `ScriptHost.members()`), the watchdog, what `find` shares,
  and the platform boundary. Every transcript was produced by the worktree binary against
  a fresh copy of `batch.pen` / `banking.pen`.
- `Tests/WoodcaseCommandTests/Help/ScriptingArticleTests.swift` — two tests, red first.
- `Tests/WoodcaseCommandTests/Help/JsTopicText.swift` — the shared reader:
  `extractScripts`/`extractOneLiners` lifted out of `JsTopicTests`, plus `blockBody`
  (which `JsDeclarationTests.Declaration` now calls instead of its own `docBlock`) and
  `declaration(in:)`, which spans `declare const doc: {` through the brace closing
  `declare class WoodcaseError`, dedented.
- Links: Woodcase.md Essentials, WoodcaseEditor.md ("When the answer is a loop" + Topics),
  WoodcaseCLI.md (`js` prose + a Scripting topic group), README.md, AGENTS.md head.
- One doc-only fix in the host: `RowPredicate.swift:71` linked
  `ScriptHost/run(_:over:remedy:diagnostics:deadline:sink:)`, a signature that does not
  exist (the real one carries `recorder:`). DocC named it; corrected.

MEASUREMENTS (all sandbox off, from the worktree)
- `swift package generate-documentation --target Woodcase`: 78 warnings before, 78 after,
  and the sorted warning texts are IDENTICAL to the baseline. Warning shapes are all
  pre-existing unresolved links — mostly `'X' doesn't exist at '/Woodcase/WoodcaseViewer'`.
- A CROSS-MODULE SYMBOL LINK DOES NOT RESOLVE. Probe: a `### Scripting` group carrying
  ``WoodcaseScripting/ScriptHost`` in Woodcase.md took the count 78 → 79, with
  `warning: 'ScriptHost' doesn't exist at '/Woodcase/WoodcaseScripting'` — the same shape
  `WoodcaseViewer.md` already has four times over. So there is NO Scripting symbol group;
  the article names the host's types in code voice and says which target they live in.
- A SECOND TRAP, worth knowing: curating `<doc:WoodcaseEditor>` and `<doc:WoodcaseCLI>` in
  the new article's own Topics took 78 → 80 with
  `Organizing 'Woodcase/WoodcaseCLI' under 'Woodcase/WoodcaseScripting' forms a cycle` —
  because both of those articles curate WoodcaseScripting. An article may not curate an
  article that curates it. They are linked from the article's prose instead, which does
  not curate. Nothing in the catalog warned about this before because no article had
  reciprocal Topics entries.
- Coverage: `swift package generate-documentation --target WoodcaseScripting
  --experimental-documentation-coverage --coverage-summary-level brief` (the brief said
  `--level brief`; that flag does not exist and docc reads the word as a catalog path and
  fails). Types 100% (13/13) abstract, Members 73% (70/96), Globals 0% (0/11). Reading
  `documentation-coverage.json`: every one of the 51 symbols without an abstract is a
  synthesized conformance member (`init(from:)`, `encode(to:)`, `hash(into:)`, `hashValue`,
  `!=`, `init(rawValue:)`), a DocC collection group, or the module page itself. No
  hand-written symbol in `Sources/WoodcaseScripting` is missing a doc comment.
  The module page has no abstract because `WoodcaseScripting` has no `.docc` catalog of
  its own — a real gap, but a new catalog is a bigger decision than this leaf; filing it
  is the integrator's call.
- `swiftformat --config <worktree>/.swiftformat --lint <worktree>`: clean, 88 files skipped
  (so the repo config was used, per the 2026-09-02 gotcha).

TDD
Both tests were red before the article existed — "the article shows 0 runnable scripts"
and "WoodcaseScripting.md carries no `declare const doc: {` block". After writing the
article I also checked that the script test BITES rather than merely passing: replacing
`doc.tree` with `doc.nope` in the article's fan-out block made it fail with the binary's
own unknown-member sentence and exit 1, then reverted.

FOR THE INTEGRATOR
`host-fixes` is changing the `.d.ts` (TreeRow gains `props?: Props`, the SEE ALSO fence
about `r.props` goes). Refresh the article's ```typescript fence from the merged
`HelpTopic+Js.swift` at merge time; `ScriptingArticleTests.theDeclarationMatchesTheTopic`
fails loudly if you forget, and names the first line that differs. The mechanical way to
do it is what I used: take the lines from `declare const doc: {` through the `}` that
closes `declare class WoodcaseError extends Error {`, dedent by the common indent, strip
trailing spaces, and paste them into the fence.

Nothing in the article restates a claim about `r.props` that the SEE ALSO change touches.

data.text:
Done on wt/host-fixes (worktree .claude/worktrees/host-fixes), not committed.

One row view, two routes. The JavaScript that builds the refusing Proxy — rowView,
propsView, PASSTHROUGH and the member list — is now Sources/WoodcaseScripting/Prelude/
RowViewPrelude.swift: a function expression taking (PATHS, DIALECT, refuse). Both
preludes interpolate that one text:

- RowPredicatePrelude keeps only what find adds — the woodcaseFind-branded refuse and
  the `doc` guard — and calls makeRowView(PATHS, 'find', refuse).
- ScriptPrelude binds `const makeRowView = <the same text>` between its vocabulary and
  its surface (a third textual chunk, the way vocabulary + surface already compose), and
  doc.tree returns rows.map(makeRowView(asked.props || [], 'js', fail)). `fail` throws
  the prelude's WoodcaseError, so a row refusal is `unknownMember` and catchable like
  every other host refusal.

RowPredicate.memberNames moved to RowViewPrelude.memberNames (one Swift constant, still
read off an encoded TreeRow); RowPredicate.install now passes only [properties], and the
one test reference was renamed.

Dialect: find's three sentences are byte-identical (RowPredicateTests unchanged except
that symbol rename). The js dialect says "this doc.tree asked for none … Pass
`props: ['kind.x']` in doc.tree's options and the same filter reads it", "A row carries
the paths the props option named and no others", and "… is read as r.props['kind.x']
with props: ['kind.x'] in doc.tree's options".

Both r.props and r.properties work on both routes; a path outside the requested columns
is refused whichever spelling is used; a requested path a row does not carry is still
undefined, not a refusal.

.d.ts (HelpTopic+Js.swift): TreeRow gains `props?: Props;  // the same bag under find's
spelling — one guarded view` beside `properties?: Props`, and the SEE ALSO fence sentence
is replaced by "A row is one value on both routes: r.props and r.properties read the same
bag, and each refuses a path the `props` option did not ask for." JsDeclarationTests and
JsTopicTests are green (the line budget still fits, and no snippet changed).

Tests, red first: Tests/WoodcaseScriptingTests/Prelude/ScriptTreeRowTests.swift (11 tests)
and Tests/WoodcaseCommandTests/Verbs/JsRowTests.swift (3 CLI tests). Watched red: the
props/member cases threw "undefined is not an object" or filtered nothing. Four of the
eleven were green before the change on purpose — they are the preservation guards the
brief asked for (a run ending in doc.tree still crosses as JSON, the rows equal the
library's own encoding, console.log renders a row, {...row} and Object.keys behave); they
would have failed had the Proxy broken stringification.

Full suite green: 4092 tests, 426 suites, `swift test --quiet`, sandbox off.
swiftformat --lint clean.

Argument-order note: doc.tree now checks its options before its address (it needs the
props list), so a call wrong in both ways reports the option first. Nothing tests that
pair, and both sentences are unchanged.

Done on wt/host-fixes (worktree .claude/worktrees/host-fixes), not committed.

The pair diff is in the library. New file Sources/Woodcase/Editing/RootOverlap+Introduced.swift:
RootOverlap.pairs(in:) (public), RootOverlap.introduced(since:in:) (public), and
RootOverlap.finding(in:file:) (public) which builds the artboard-overlap LintFinding.
RootOverlap.roots gained a package overload taking an already-settled tree, and
pairs(in:settled:) is package for the same reason — SettledTree is a `package` type, so a
public signature cannot name it.

ScriptRunner snapshots the pairs at the top of run(_:) through its own SettledTreeCache,
so a script that reads at all gets the snapshot for the settle its first read was going to
pay for anyway (SettledTreeCacheTests' "two reads settle once" is still 1). At the end of
the run, after the last source and only when the run both reached the end and wrote, it
records one event per newly overlapping pair. A run that ends in an error records none:
nothing was written, so there is no overlap on disk to warn about — that is a behaviour
change, see below.

DECISION the brief asked for: ScriptRun.Event.warning(String) is unchanged and a sibling
case `overlap(LintFinding)` carries the finding. Reasons: LintFormatter and LintFinding
are both in the Woodcase library, so a library caller (Penumbra) gets the structured fact
and can render the identical line itself; and the CLI keeps the line byte-identical
without sniffing strings — ScriptRunFormatter renders `.warning` as "warning  <text>" (its
own gutter) and `.overlap` as the text alone, which is already
"warning artboard-overlap  …". Changing warning's payload instead would have made every
existing warning carry a wrapper for one new case.

JsCommand no longer diffs: Body and RolledBack lost their `warnings` field,
RootOverlapWarnings.pairs/lines are no longer called from `js`, and ScriptRunReport builds
`warnings` from the run's overlap events. Printing: in text mode the live sink prints each
overlap as it is recorded; under --json the sink is off, so the same lines are written to
stderr once from the report. Verified by hand in both modes — one line on stderr, one
entry in `warnings`, and (new) one `{"event":"overlap","text":…}` in `events`.

## Part 2 — font cache premise check (verdict: false as stated; built nothing)

The issue's specific claim: "a second suite placing JetBrains Mono mid-run
can flip `GoogleFontResolverTests`' absent-to-present transition" via the
shared `~/Library/Caches/woodcase` cache. This does not hold, for two
independent reasons, both checked directly:

1. **No test reads the real cache.** `grep -rn "GoogleFontCache()" Tests` and
   `grep -rn "GoogleFontResolver.shared" Tests` both return zero matches.
   Every test that builds a `GoogleFontCache` passes an explicit
   `rootDirectory: tempDir` (`GoogleFontResolverTests.swift`,
   `GoogleFontCacheTests.swift`, `SettledFontPreparationTests.swift`) — fully
   isolated from `~/Library/Caches/com.bensyverson.woodcase/fonts/`, the
   directory `GoogleFontCache.defaultCacheDirectory()` resolves to
   (`Sources/Woodcase/GoogleFonts/GoogleFontCache.swift:38-47`, via
   `FileManager.default.url(for: .cachesDirectory, …)`).

2. **CoreText registration cannot cross a process boundary regardless.**
   `CommandFixture.run(_:)` (`Tests/WoodcaseCommandTests/Support/CommandFixture.swift:94-128`)
   spawns the built `woodcase` binary as a real, separate OS `Process`. When
   such a run drives `shot`/`render`, it does exercise the **real** font
   cache in that *subprocess* — `RenderCommand.swift:90` and
   `ShotCommand.swift:324` call `GoogleFontResolver.shared`, whose lazy
   singleton (`GoogleFontResolver.swift:41-48`) falls back to
   `GoogleFontCache()` (no `rootDirectory` argument) when it can be
   constructed, i.e. the real `~/Library/Caches/...` path — and
   `CommandFixture.environment(adding:)` overriding `HOME` to the fixture's
   temp root does **not** redirect this, exactly as gotchas.md (2026-09-02)
   already records: `.cachesDirectory` resolves via `getpwuid`, not `$HOME`.
   But `CTFontManagerRegisterFontsForURL(…, .process, …)` registers into
   *that subprocess's* Core Text registry, which is a different OS process
   from the `swift test` host running `GoogleFontResolverTests` — it cannot
   place a family into this process's registry. This is exactly what the
   dispatch note already predicted ("CoreText font registration is
   process-scoped, so a second process cannot register a family into this
   one"), now checked against the actual `Process()`-based fixture rather
   than assumed.

   `grep -rln "JetBrains Mono" Tests Sources` finds it in exactly two
   places: `GoogleFontResolverTests.swift` (the owning test) and
   `Sources/WoodcaseViewer/Styles/ViewerStylesheet.swift:64`, which is a CSS
   `font-family` fallback list rendered by the browser — never walked by
   `GoogleFontResolver.collectFontFamilies(from:)`, so it never enters the
   font-resolution pipeline at all. No CommandFixture fixture or test
   references the family, so no subprocess run ever writes it into the real
   cache in the first place; this is doubly moot even before the
   process-boundary argument.

3. **The broader "does a write change what another process observes"
   question, checked anyway:** CommandFixture-driven `shot`/`render` runs on
   fixtures that *do* name a non-system Google Font (if any exist) would
   write into the shared real disk cache — a genuine, if narrow, form of
   cross-run state. But no test's assertions depend on which font actually
   got resolved (`grep` for `fontFamily|font-family|Google|MAE|mae` across
   every CommandFixture test that runs `shot`/`render` turns up nothing
   pipeline-relevant), so even that write changes no test's pass/fail. There
   is nothing here that meets the brief's bar for fixing ("only if a test
   provably reads the real cache in a way another process can change").

**Verdict: built nothing for part 2.** The premise as stated in the issue
(the JetBrains Mono absent→present flip) is false; refuted with the
evidence above rather than worked around.

## Deviations from the brief

- None substantive. The brief's TDD framing ("watch it fail") turned out to
  mean a *build* failure rather than a runtime test failure, since the type
  under test didn't exist yet — noted above, not a deviation, just how "red"
  looked here.
- One test assertion (`URL ==` across `deletingLastPathComponent()`) needed
  a `.path`-based comparison instead of `URL`-based; this was a bug in the
  *test I wrote*, not a brief issue, fixed before considering it green.
- The first full-suite run wedged (DpQmXu) under three-way load and the
  coordinator killed it mid-flight; my own tooling (Bash `run_in_background`
  plus a `Monitor` polling `kill -0`) reported it as a clean exit-0 pass,
  which was wrong — `kill -0` under Monitor's own sandbox (no
  disable-sandbox option there) silently fails as "permission denied" and
  reads as "process gone" even for a still-running PID, so my "is it done"
  polling was unreliable throughout. Re-ran per the coordinator's explicit
  correction (no `--quiet`, logged to `local/`, sandbox off) and got real
  results this time. Worth a harness gotcha: `Monitor` cannot check process
  liveness with `kill -0` under its default sandbox; poll via `ps` (Bash,
  sandbox off) instead, or just trust the originating `run_in_background`
  task's own completion notification rather than adding a second watcher.

## What's wrong in the brief

- Part 2's premise (JetBrains Mono absent→present flip from a second suite)
  does not hold, as analyzed above — this was flagged as an open question in
  the brief itself and the dispatch note already suspected as much; this
  note is the confirmation with file:line evidence.
- Minor: `swift test --quiet --filter <X>` on a **build failure** (as opposed
  to a runtime test failure) prints only `error: fatalError` with no
  filename/line — matches the harness note about editing-during-build, but
  here the cause was a genuinely undefined symbol, not a mid-build edit. A
  future TDD-red check that expects a *build* failure should drop `--quiet`
  the first time to see the real diagnostic, or expect a bare `fatalError`
  as normal red-by-build rather than red-by-assertion.

data.title: One rule for a leading `$` across content, override and escaping
data.description:
Text content forgives a bare `$name` that matches no variable and keeps the literal;
the same string through an instance override is an `unresolved-variable` error; and
escaping it as `\$` mid-string prints a literal backslash. Three behaviours for one
character, split by which verb wrote it (Nanoshoot N, three prices). The rule to adopt
everywhere is content's rule exactly: forgive a `$name` **only when no variable of
that name exists** in the document, so a `$name` that matches a real variable still
resolves — or still lints as unresolved when it is themed away — as it does today;
this must not become a way to hide a genuine dangling reference. Make the escape
consume its backslash on both routes, and say the rule once in `override --help`.
Finding: DX item 5 of project/2026-09-08-scripting-host-trial-2.md.

"add" a variable that already exists silently recolours every reference (round two C:

data.title: Five message fixes from round two
data.description:
(1) `tree <ref> --props kind.content` on a bare instance says the property grammar;
when every row in the listing is a ref with no children shown, say `--expand` (A, C).
(2) The `cp` placement note names the source when the copy was renamed in the same
call; name the copy (B, C). (3) The `apply` refusal for a line that is not valid JSON
says the grammar; when the line is a fragment of a multi-line object, say one op per
line (N). (4) A `find` predicate written as a bare expression fails with `Can't find
variable: r`; when the text is not a function and evaluating it throws a reference
error on a bare identifier, say that a predicate is a function of one row, `r => …`
(N). (5) `get --help` says that `--json` nests the node under `node` beside

and 7 and sentences 3 and 4 of project/2026-09-08-scripting-host-trial-2.md.

data.description:
Themed colours cannot go through `apply`: the `var` op refuses anything but
`{type,value}`, so a 17-colour, two-option token layer is 34 process launches through
a shell loop (Nanoshoot N). Let the op carry the themed form `vars set --theme`
accepts, and let `vars set` take several `name=value` pairs in one call. Finding: DX
item 5 of project/2026-09-08-scripting-host-trial-2.md. Extends WoodcaseBatches.md.

data.title: `help design` hands a measure-and-fix loop to `js` in one sentence
data.description:
This is the one item in the list with a stance rather than a fix. Round two's control
agent read the primer's paragraph on `js` and still did its measure-and-fix loop as
eleven transactions of single writes and reads; under Ben's framing that is an
acceptable instinct, but eleven transactions where one would do is a real cost to the
user. The paragraph describes `js`; it does not say *when a loop of writes and reads
is what you are about to do, that loop is a `js` program*. One sentence in the
read-write-verify section of `help design`, in that shape, plus the same in
WoodcaseEditor.md's "When the answer is a loop". It is a nudge, and only a third round
with an unprimed agent says whether it worked. Finding:
project/2026-09-08-scripting-host-trial-2.md, the instinct finding.

The leaf's premise is wrong in one place, and the real bug is next door.

`BatchOperation.VariableOp.value` is a `PenVariable`, whose `PenVariableValue`
decoder already tries `[PenThemedValue]` before a scalar. So the themed shape
DECODED before this change — verified against the pre-change binary on
2026-09-08:

    woodcase apply t.pen -F b.jsonl --as ana
    line 0  applied  document
    1 applied, 0 failed, 0 cascaded — revision ef54dea8ede0e971

with b.jsonl holding
    {"op":"var","name":"accent","value":{"type":"color","value":[
      {"value":"#ffffff","theme":{"mode":"light"}},
      {"value":"#000000","theme":{"mode":"dark"}}]}}   (one line)

What it did NOT do is register the axis. After that line, `woodcase themes t.pen`
said "No themes defined" while `variables.accent` was conditioned on
`mode=light` / `mode=dark` — a document `vars set --theme` can never produce and
nothing can select. That is the state Nanoshoot N would have landed in had it
tried the shape it reported as refused; its shell loop over `vars set --theme`
avoided the trap by accident.

So the fix delivered is the registration, not a decoder: `planVariable` now runs
`ThemeAxisRegistrar.registrations(for:in:)` — the same rule, in one place, that
`vars set --theme` uses — and emits the axis edits ahead of the variable edit.
`doc.vars.set` in the JS host writes through the same `var` op, so it gains the
registration too.

Second choice, recorded because it is a two-way door: the `var` line still
REPLACES the whole value rather than merging one pin into what is there. A
merging line would need a `theme` field beside `value` and would make `var` two
grammars; a batch line that carries every variant is the bulk route the leaf
asked for (17 lines, not 34), and `vars set --theme` remains the merge. Said so
in the grammar and in WoodcaseBatches.md.

Seam chosen, and why not the one the leaf named.

Neither `BareOptionValue.filled` nor `ParserFailureMessage` is the place.

- `BareOptionValue.filled` REWRITES the vector. Anything it does to
  `--accent=#e0561a` makes it work silently, which the leaf forbids, and its own
  DocC says it is deliberately a table of one — an option belongs there only when
  writing it bare is a request a verb can answer.
- `ParserFailureMessage` rewords `PenParserError` — a .pen file that will not
  decode. It never sees an ArgumentParser failure.

The seam used is `WoodcaseCommand.exitReportingHouseCode`, on the
`.validationFailure` branch, given the argument vector `main()` already built.
It fires only after the parse has ALREADY failed, so it can never shadow an
invocation that works, and the new `SeparatorRemedy` decides whether this
particular failure is the one.

The discriminator is the interesting part. A table of `vars set`'s options would
drift the first time one was added, and the naive rule ("a `--name=value` token
before any `--`") is wrong: `--type=color` is that shape, is a correctly spelled
option, and repairing it would tell the caller to write a variable literally
named `--type`. So `SeparatorRemedy.isName` asks the parser instead — it parses
`["vars","set","probe.pen","probe=1", token]`, a complete line but for the token.
If that parses, the token is one of the verb's own options and the failure lies
elsewhere; if it does not, it is a variable name. `PenFilePath` never touches
disk at parse time, so the probe path is free.

Held by `SeparatorRemedyTests`, whose second half is the load-bearing one: a
correctly spelled `--type=color` must keep ArgumentParser's own message.

Shape of the announcement, and the reference walk.

Text, one line before the outline:

  --accent already existed with 14 refs, as color * #f5f5f5, Mode=Dark #262626 —
  this write changes what all 14 of them resolve to.

A themed old value lists every variant, `pin value`, in file order (`*` is the
fallback), because the caller is about to replace one and keep the rest. A plain
value prints bare. `0 refs` drops the trailing clause — there is nothing the
write changes.

JSON: `previous`, an array of the same `VariableFormatter.Row` shape `vars list`
prints, holding only the names that already existed; absent entirely when every
name in the call was fresh. A field, not a sentence, and one a caller branches on
by `previous[i].references.nodes`.

Reference counting reuses `vars list`'s index, not a second walk. It could not
reuse it as it stood: `VariableFormatter.row(for:in:)` called
`document.references(to:)`, which calls `variableReferences()` — a re-encode of
every node — once PER NAME. A seventeen-pair call would have walked the document
seventeen times for the pre-state and seventeen more for the post-state. So
`VariableFormatter.rows(for:in:)` now takes the whole name list and walks once,
and `row(for:in:)` is a one-element call into it. Same index, same counts as
`vars list`.

The pre-state is read before the axes are registered and before any value is
written, so the counts a caller is warned with are the counts the OLD value had.

Mechanism confirmed in `PenLayoutEngine.layoutLeafNode`: a leaf's width is resolved from
`kind.width` alone; a measurement only overrides it when `textGrowth` says the axis
should follow the text (`needsWidthFromText` excludes `fixed-width`; `fixed-width-height`
skips all measurement). A `fit_content` width/height with no numeric fallback then
resolves to 0 (`resolveIntrinsicSize` returns `fallback ?? 0`). This is the same "nothing
to fall back on" shape as `fill-in-fit-parent`/`empty-fit-content`, applied to text
growth instead of container children.

Implemented all five message fixes. TDD: wrote all 12 new/changed assertions first,
confirmed RED (12 issues, exactly the new tests, 71 others unaffected), then implemented.

Brief error found: fix (2)'s "cp placement note" is not composed in
Sources/WoodcaseCommandCore/Reports (OutsideWriteNote.swift / CreatedTreeFormatter.swift,
the brief's candidates) — it is built by BatchApplier+Divergence.swift's
`placement(of:from:coordinates:)`, called from BatchApplier+Create.swift's
`planCopyInsert`, both under the `BatchApplier*.swift` glob the brief puts off limits
(owned by the vars-dx agent). The bug is real: `planCopyInsert` computes the divergence
from the copy's node *before* its own command-line properties (including a `common.name`
rename) are applied in the same plan, so the note names the pre-rename (source-carried)
name. Fixed at the CLI layer instead — a new Sources/WoodcaseCommandCore/Reports/
CopyPlacementNote.swift rewrites a `.rootPlacement` divergence's target/note from the
settled document after the write, called from CopyCommand.swift. Scoped to a single copy
(`copy.id != nil`); `--times`/`--each` divergences are untouched because the result carries
no id-to-divergence mapping for a multi-root write without a BatchApplier-side change. Real
fix belongs beside the sentence, in BatchApplier+Create.swift/+Divergence.swift, next time
that file is not contended.

All 5 fixes verified against the real built binary (.build/…/debug/woodcase), not just the
test assertions, before finalizing wording.

Done on branch wt/hermetic-fonts (worktree .claude/worktrees/hermetic-fonts), 2026-09-08.

WHAT CHANGED. `RenderCache.init` now takes `fonts: GoogleFontResolver = .shared` and
`images: RemoteImageResolver = .shared`, and `prepare` uses them instead of reaching for
the singletons — the same shape `SettledTree(fontResolver:)` already had. Production
wiring is untouched: `ViewerServer.swift:95` and the `serve`/`preview` verbs still write
`RenderCache()` and still fetch, which is right for a rendering surface. All 20
`RenderCache()` in Tests/WoodcaseViewerTests now go through a new
`ViewerFixtures.renders()`, over one target-wide resolver pair whose fetcher
(`OfflineFetcher`) throws without opening a socket and whose caches are rooted at a temp
path that is never created. New `HermeticNetworkTests` (WoodcaseTests) scans Tests/ for
`URLSessionDataFetcher`, `GoogleFontResolver.shared`, `RemoteImageResolver.shared` and
for any `RenderCache(...)` that does not name `fonts:`, with a two-entry allowlist that
carries a sentence each.

BASELINE — WHICH TESTS FAIL WITHOUT INTER: none.
- Before the change, `WOODCASE_HOME=<empty> swift test --filter WoodcaseViewerTests`
  passed (446 tests) AND left `<empty>/fonts/inter/Inter[opsz,wght].ttf` behind — proof
  the suite downloads 880 KB from GitHub on every run.
- After the change, the same command passes 446 tests, prints one
  `woodcase: Font 'Inter' could not be resolved; will fall back to SF Pro`, and leaves
  the directory EMPTY. So no viewer assertion or golden depends on Inter's metrics; no
  fixture had to be repointed at IBM Plex Sans and no golden was regenerated.
- I could not run the viewer target with the network genuinely unavailable to the
  process: the fetcher cannot be swapped from outside, and macOS offers no per-process
  network off switch without root. The empty-cache-directory result is the proof
  instead, and it is a stronger one — it shows no fetch was attempted, not that one
  failed.

CLI EXPOSURE (out of scope for code, per the brief). Each `CommandFixture` hands the
child process its own fresh empty `$WOODCASE_HOME`, so a shot/render test does not merely
reuse a cached font — it re-downloads one per test. Static scan
(scratch/CNDISf-cli-exposure.py) over the 12 CLI test files that run shot/render:
- `Tests/WoodcaseCommandTests/Verbs/ShotComponentTests.swift` — 6 tests: 3 over
  banking.pen (Inter) and 3 over woodcase-app.pen (`$font-primary` → IBM Plex Sans).
  Verified by hand: `WOODCASE_HOME=<empty> .build/debug/woodcase shot
  Tests/WoodcaseTests/Fixtures/banking.pen banking-home --out <dir>` writes
  `<empty>/fonts/inter/Inter[opsz,wght].ttf`; the same over woodcase-app.pen and
  "Home - Collection (Dark)" writes `fonts/ibmplexsans/IBMPlexSans[wdth,wght].ttf`.
- `Tests/WoodcaseCommandTests/Help/DesignTopicClaimsTests.swift` — 1 shot over
  font-missing.pen ("Woodcase No Such Face"): no download, but three METADATA.pb probes
  to raw.githubusercontent.com that must all 404 before the fallback line appears. That
  test's assertion is *about* the fallback, so behind a captive portal it passes for the
  wrong reason and behind a slow one it waits on URLSession's seven-day resource timeout.
- The other 10 shot/render test files use fixtures whose only families are system faces,
  so they cost nothing.
Total: 7 tests, 6 downloads per full-suite run, plus 3 failing probes.
RECOMMENDATION: not an environment knob and not an offline mode — those are product
decisions. Two cheap options, in order of preference: (a) repoint ShotComponentTests at a
fixture whose families the machine already has, since none of those six tests is about
type at all (they are about component addressing and --outline); (b) give CommandFixture
a seeded `$WOODCASE_HOME/fonts` copied from Tests/WoodcaseTests/Fonts, which makes the

before the change; the fetcher scan was reddened by temporarily removing
PenRemoteImageProviderTests from the allowlist, which named it; the allowlist-currency
test reddened at the same moment. All three green after.

TRAP WORTH KNOWING. A source-scan test must read code, not prose: the first full-suite
run failed because OfflineRenderCache.swift's own doc comment *explains* the forbidden
`RenderCache()` shape. `sources()` now drops whole-line comments (only those — stripping
to end-of-line would cut `https://` inside a string literal and hide what followed).

Done on wt/dollar-rule. One rule for `$`, fixed at the source rather than in the lint.

What changed
- New `PenDollarEscape` (Sources/Woodcase/Models/PenDollarEscape.swift) states the escape
  once: `\$` is read anywhere in the string, and written only in front of a *leading* `$`,
  because only a leading `$` is ambiguous on the wire. A `$` further in is stored bare, so a
  reader with no escape convention still sees text.
- `PenValue<String>` decode/encode now goes through it, so a mid-string `\$` loses its
  backslash on both the content route and the override route (the override's raw string is
  merged into the node's JSON and decoded by `PenValue` at expansion).
- `PenVariableResolver` now carries `definedNames` into a ref's `descendants` and
  `rootOverrides`, and applies text content's forgiveness to the `content` key there: a
  `$name` the document defines nowhere is written back escaped, which is the wire form of the
  literal it almost certainly was. Nothing in the lint needed changing — `collectReferences`
  simply stops seeing a `$`-prefixed string.
- Forgiveness did not widen: the key set is `["content"]` alone, and a name the document DOES
  define still resolves, or still lints unresolved when nothing resolves it.

Findings worth keeping
- The brief's hypothesis was right: rendering was already identical on both routes
  (`PenRefExpander` applies the override before resolution). Only lint differed. The
  render-parity test was green on first run and is kept as a regression guard.
- "Themed away" is not a reachable state. `buildTable` falls back to the *first* themed
  variant when no theme matches, so a variable defined only for `mode=dark` still resolves
  under `light`. The honest defined-but-unresolvable case is a circular chain, which the
  resolver drops from the table; the tests use that.
- `PenPipelineTests.oldPipelineOrderBug` had to change: it *documented* the resolve-then-
  expand bug (`$186` becoming `.variable("186")`). The resolver fix removes that hazard, so
  both pipeline orders now agree; the test asserts the agreement instead.
- `BatchApplier+Divergence.swift` needs no change. Its `$` echo fires only for a name the
  document defines, which is exactly right under the new rule.
- `help design`'s VALUES paragraph does need replacing — exact text is in the report.
